title: Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D.
backgroundAndFacts:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued guidance allowing immigration authorities to remove noncitizens to third countries—meaning countries other than the person's home country—without first giving those individuals notice of where they were being sent or a meaningful chance to claim they would face persecution or torture there. This policy affected people who had already received final orders of removal but who, under longstanding law, could not simply be sent anywhere without certain protections.

A group of affected noncitizens, identified only by their initials to protect their safety, sued the government in federal district court in Massachusetts. The district court sided with the plaintiffs in February 2026, issuing a broad ruling that blocked the government's third-country removal guidance and granted relief to an entire class of similarly situated people. The court found that the guidance violated federal immigration law, constitutional due process rights, and regulations implementing the international Convention Against Torture (CAT).

The government appealed, and the First Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the district court's ruling in September 2026. DHS then sought emergency relief from the Supreme Court, which agreed to take the case on an expedited basis. The Court stayed the lower court's order while the case proceeds, meaning the government may continue implementing its third-country removal policy during the litigation. Three justices—Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson—would have denied the stay.
legalQuestion: Whether the government's policy of removing noncitizens to third countries (countries other than their home country) without individualized notice or an opportunity to seek protection violates federal immigration statutes, the Due Process Clause, and international anti-torture obligations.
significance:
This case has sweeping implications for the rights of noncitizens facing deportation and the limits of executive power in immigration enforcement. At its core, the case asks whether the government can remove people to countries they have no ties to—potentially dangerous ones—without giving them any warning or a chance to argue they would be tortured or persecuted there. A ruling for the government could dramatically expand its deportation options; a ruling for the respondents could require individualized procedural protections before any third-country removal.

The case also raises major structural questions about judicial power in immigration cases. The Supreme Court will decide whether federal courts can even hear these kinds of challenges and, if so, whether they can issue sweeping class-wide relief blocking a government policy entirely. The outcome could reshape how courts oversee immigration enforcement actions and how far the Administrative Procedure Act's remedies extend in the immigration context.

parties.party: Department of Homeland Security, et al.
parties.coreArgument: The government argues that the district court lacked jurisdiction to hear these claims under a federal statute that strips courts of authority to enjoin or restrain the operation of removal orders on a class-wide basis. Even if jurisdiction existed, the court had no power to issue broad declaratory relief or vacate agency guidance for an entire class of people, and the third-country removal guidance is lawful under the relevant statutes and regulations.
supportingPoints: 8 U.S.C. §1252(f)(1) expressly prohibits lower federal courts from granting classwide injunctive or equitable relief that interferes with the government's authority to carry out removal orders.
The government's third-country removal guidance complies with 8 U.S.C. §1231(b), which gives DHS broad discretion to choose the country of removal when the designated country is unavailable.
Due process does not require individualized notice and hearing before every third-country removal because noncitizens with final removal orders have already received extensive procedural protections.
The Convention Against Torture and its implementing regulations do not entitle every removable noncitizen to a pre-removal hearing on third-country torture claims absent a threshold showing of risk.

parties.coreArgument: The respondents argue that the government cannot lawfully remove people to third countries without first notifying them of the intended destination and giving them a genuine opportunity to raise safety concerns, including claims of potential torture or persecution. They contend that the district court had jurisdiction, that class-wide relief was appropriate, and that the government's guidance violates both federal statutes and the Constitution.
supportingPoints: Federal immigration law and the Convention Against Torture require that individuals facing removal have notice and an opportunity to present evidence that they would be tortured or persecuted in any proposed country of removal, including third countries.

The due process rights of the respondents—some of whom have lived in the United States for many years—require meaningful procedural protections before being sent to a country with which they may have no connection and where they may face grave danger.

Section 1252(f)(1) does not bar the district court's declaratory judgment or APA vacatur because those forms of relief are distinct from injunctions and are expressly permitted under the Administrative Procedure Act.

Class-wide relief was necessary and appropriate because the government's guidance affected a large group of similarly situated individuals who would otherwise have no effective way to vindicate their rights individually before being removed.

citedPrecedents.reasonCited: This case directly interpreted the scope of 8 U.S.C. §1252(f)(1), holding that the provision strips lower courts of jurisdiction to issue class-wide injunctions against the operation of removal statutes.

The government cites this case for the proposition that noncitizens in expedited removal proceedings have limited constitutional rights to judicial review and that Congress may restrict court access in immigration cases.

This foundational due process case provides the balancing test courts use to determine what procedural protections are constitutionally required before the government deprives someone of a liberty or property interest.

Respondents cite this case for the principle that noncitizens with final removal orders retain meaningful legal rights and that courts must interpret immigration statutes to avoid rendering those rights illusory.

This case is relevant to the jurisdictional question because it established that courts should not read immigration statutes to eliminate all meaningful judicial review of removal orders absent a clear statement from Congress.

This case addressed government transfers of individuals to foreign countries and the limits of judicial intervention, which is relevant to the question of what protections are required before transferring someone to a country where they may face mistreatment.
